title: The clever steward (Luke 16:1–13)
hook: a crooked manager is praised for being shrewd; you can't serve God and mammon

segments.voice: Yesterday, a builder sat down to count before he built his tower. Your line was sit down and reckon.

A manager is caught wasting his boss's money. He's about to be fired. So he spends his last afternoon cooking the books in his customers' favor. And at the end of the story, the boss praises him. This is a parable preachers sometimes approach carefully, and readers still argue about parts of it. It sounds like Jesus is applauding fraud. He isn't. To see what he is doing, watch the manager's hands.
screen: `A PARABLE READERS STILL ARGUE ABOUT.` → `CAUGHT WASTING THE BOSS'S MONEY.` → `AND THE BOSS PRAISES HIM.`

segments.voice: A rich man hears his steward has wasted his goods. He calls him in: give an account, you're done. The steward thinks fast. I can't dig, I'm ashamed to beg. I know what I'll do, so that people will take me into their homes. He calls in his master's debtors one by one. How much do you owe? A hundred barrels of oil. Sit down quickly, write fifty. And you? A hundred quarters of wheat. Write eighty. He's making friends with the only currency he has left. Then the surprise: "And the lord commended the unjust steward, forasmuch as he had done wisely: for the children of this world are wiser in their generation than the children of light." Notice what's praised. Not the dishonesty; he's still called unjust. He saw the end coming and acted. He knew his position wouldn't last, and he used what was passing through his hands to make friends who would. Jesus draws the lesson: make friends with the mammon of iniquity, so that when you fail, when your own time runs out, they may receive you into everlasting dwellings. Mammon is the Douay's word for wealth, money and property. In the Catholic reading, everyone is a steward like this one, who will one day be asked to give an account. So use it now, while it's in your hands, for people. Then the line the passage ends on: "You cannot serve God and mammon." No servant can serve two masters.
screen: `GIVE AN ACCOUNT. YOU'RE DONE.` · `A HUNDRED BARRELS? WRITE FIFTY.` · `PRAISED FOR SEEING THE END COMING.` · `WHEN YOU FAIL, FRIENDS RECEIVE YOU.` · then, large: `YOU CANNOT SERVE GOD AND MAMMON.`

segments.voice: Picture what's passing through your hands this week, a paycheck, an allowance, a budget, even a few dollars, and notice that none of it stays. Think of one person you could do some good for with a small part of it: a coworker's lunch, a friend's coffee, a family that's struggling. If you pray, ask to be a faithful steward.
Mammon. The Douay's word for wealth, money and property, what the crooked steward used to make friends before his time ran out. Today's word.
Your line: god or mammon. What you hold, you won't hold forever. That's day four hundred seventy-one.

howItsDone: Catholics often speak of stewardship, the idea that time, talent and money are entrusted by God rather than owned outright, and some parishes ask members to make an annual stewardship commitment.

original.note: Greek, from Aramaic mamona: wealth, property, what a person trusts in.

trapdoor: what you thought: this parable says a little fraud is fine if it's clever.
what it means: the steward is still unjust; he's praised for seeing his time is short and using money to make lasting friends.
what a scholar hears: in verse 8 Luke calls the master kyrios, the same word he uses for Jesus, which is part of why readers still argue over who does the praising.
recall: flowers that never labor or spin

chat.says: Why does the boss praise a steward who cheated him?
options: Not for cheating: he saw his end coming and used money to make friends.
Because cutting debts in half is always good, whatever the reason.
Because the boss secretly told him to cut those debts all along.
chat.meaning: He's still called unjust; what's praised is that he saw the end coming and used what passed through his hands for people.
